investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why has the skull X-ray been largely abandoned for head injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: CT head detects intracranial injury (haemorrhage, contusion) and guides management; a skull fracture on plain film neither confirms nor excludes brain injury and rarely changes management. NICE head injury guidance triages to CT, not skull X-ray. A normal skull film does not reassure.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Name the remaining/niche indications for a plain skull X-ray.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Suspected non-accidental injury (part of paediatric skeletal survey), localising radio-opaque foreign bodies, certain metabolic/bone diseases (myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, Paget's, thalassaemia), assessing the sella turcica (historically pituitary tumour, now MRI), and shunt series for VP shunt integrity.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you distinguish a vault fracture from a suture or vascular marking on skull X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A fracture is a sharp, straight, non-branching lucent line that crosses suture lines and vascular grooves. Sutures run in fixed anatomical positions with a serrated edge; vascular markings branch and taper.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Match the classic skull X-ray pattern to its disease.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: "Punched-out" lytic lesions = multiple myeloma; "pepperpot"/salt-and-pepper = hyperparathyroidism; "cotton wool" sclerosis / osteoporosis circumscripta = Paget's disease; "hair-on-end" = thalassaemia (marrow expansion).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which standard views make up a skull series and what does each show?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: PA/AP (frontal vault, orbits), lateral (vault, sella turcica, sinuses, calcification), and Towne's view (angled AP projecting the occiput for occipital fractures).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which plain radiograph views are standard for assessing the facial skeleton in trauma?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The occipitomental (OM / "Waters") views taken at 15° and 30° — best for the orbits, maxillary sinuses, zygomatic arches and facial skeleton. CT is now definitive for complex mid-face and orbital injuries.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the three McGrigor–Campbell lines used to review a facial X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Line 1: across the zygomatico-frontal sutures and superior orbital margins. Line 2: across the zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra. Line 3: across the mandibular condyles and occlusal line. Compare left with right for asymmetry.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is an orbital "blowout" fracture and its classic radiographic sign?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A fracture of the orbital floor with herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus. It produces the "teardrop" sign hanging into the antral roof, often with opacification or a fluid level in the maxillary antrum, plus enophthalmos and diplopia with restricted upgaze from inferior rectus tethering.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does a fluid level in the maxillary sinus after facial trauma suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A haemoantrum (blood in the sinus), which strongly implies an underlying facial fracture. Soft-tissue emphysema is another indirect sign of communication with an air-containing sinus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the Le Fort fracture classifications of the mid-face?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Le Fort I: low transverse fracture of the maxilla. Le Fort II: pyramidal fracture involving the nasal bridge and infraorbital rims. Le Fort III: complete craniofacial disjunction separating the mid-face from the skull base. All warrant CT facial bones.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Is a nasal X-ray indicated for a suspected simple isolated nasal fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: No. A simple nasal fracture is a clinical diagnosis. NICE/ENT practice is not to routinely X-ray — the film is unreliable and does not change management. Assess and manage clinically.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the must-not-miss bedside finding after nasal trauma, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A septal haematoma — a boggy swelling on the nasal septum found by examining inside the nose. If missed it causes septal cartilage necrosis/abscess and a saddle-nose deformity. It needs urgent incision and drainage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: When should a displaced nasal fracture be reviewed and manipulated?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Review at ~5–7 days once swelling settles to judge deformity. Manipulation (MUA) should be done within ~10–14 days (2 weeks) of injury, before the bones set.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Clear fluid rhinorrhoea after nasal/facial trauma — significance and correct investigation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Suggests a cribriform plate / anterior skull base fracture with a CSF leak. Confirm with beta-2-transferrin (halo/tramline sign clinically). Requires CT and neurosurgical input — NOT a nasal X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: If a nasal X-ray is ever performed, which views are used?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Lateral nasal bones and occipitomental (OM) views — but these are rarely indicated, as normal sutures/grooves mimic fractures and imaging does not alter management.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What single view does an OPG (DPT) provide, and what structures does it show?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A panoramic (curved-plane tomographic) image showing the whole mandible, maxilla, all teeth and both TMJs on one film. Used for mandibular fractures, dental caries/abscess, impacted/wisdom teeth, jaw cysts/tumours, osteomyelitis, TMJ and pre-extraction planning.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why are mandibular fractures often found in two places?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The mandible is a bony ring (like a polo mint). A rigid ring struck in one place tends to break in a second place, so fractures are frequently bilateral — always look for a second fracture. Classic pairing: a body/parasymphyseal fracture with a contralateral condylar or angle fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List the radiographic/clinical signs of a mandibular fracture on an OPG.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A lucent fracture line, a step or break in the (lower-border) cortex, clinical malocclusion, and a tooth lying within the fracture line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which mandibular fracture pattern threatens the airway, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A bilateral anterior/parasymphyseal ('bucket-handle') fracture — the free anterior fragment and tongue can fall backwards and obstruct the airway. It is an emergency requiring urgent airway management.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a fracture through the tooth-bearing part of the mandible significant, and what extra view supplements the OPG?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It communicates with the mouth, making it an open (compound) fracture that needs antibiotics and maxillofacial referral. The OPG foreshortens the condyles, so it is supplemented by a PA mandible or reverse-Towne's view.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the three classic indications for a lateral soft tissue neck X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: (1) Suspected radio-opaque foreign body / impacted bone in the pharynx or upper oesophagus; (2) suspected upper airway infection in a child (croup vs epiglottitis vs retropharyngeal abscess); (3) assessing prevertebral soft tissue swelling. It also shows surgical emphysema.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the 'thumbprint sign' and why must you be cautious about obtaining it?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A swollen, rounded epiglottis on the lateral neck film indicating epiglottitis. Epiglottitis is a clinical airway emergency — do not distress the child or force an X-ray; secure the airway first with senior anaesthetic/ENT help.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is the 'steeple sign' NOT seen on a lateral soft tissue neck film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The steeple sign is subglottic narrowing from croup and is a frontal (AP/PA) view sign, not a lateral one. Croup causes barking cough and stridor, usually in a well-appearing younger child.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What radiographic findings suggest a retropharyngeal abscess?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Widened prevertebral soft tissues (wider than the adjacent vertebral body; rough rule >~7 mm at C2, >~14–22 mm at C6), sometimes with gas or an air-fluid level. The child characteristically holds the neck extended. Needs urgent ENT referral.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why must a lateral soft tissue neck film be taken in inspiration with the neck extended?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Flexion or expiration falsely widens the prevertebral soft tissues and can mimic a retropharyngeal collection. Always confirm correct technique before calling prevertebral swelling — a common pitfall.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which imaging modality does NICE/modern practice favour over plain films in significant cervical spine trauma, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: CT cervical spine — plain films miss clinically significant injuries. CT is more sensitive and is the investigation of choice in significant trauma.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Name the two clinical decision rules used to decide who needs cervical spine imaging.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The Canadian C-Spine Rule and NEXUS. NEXUS clears the neck if all five low-risk criteria are met (no midline tenderness, no focal deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no distracting injury).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: On the lateral cervical film, what defines an ADEQUATE film and what are the four alignment lines?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Adequacy: C1 must be visualised down to the C7/T1 junction. The four lines are the anterior vertebral body line, posterior vertebral body line, spinolaminar line, and the tips of the spinous processes.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does the 'ABCS' systematic approach to the cervical lateral stand for?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Adequacy (C7/T1 seen), Alignment (four lines + lordosis), Bone (each vertebra/cortex/fractures), Cartilage (disc/interspinous spaces), Soft tissues (prevertebral widening from blood/oedema).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Match the injury: axial-load burst of the C1 ring / bilateral C2 pars fracture from hyperextension / avulsed C7 spinous process.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Jefferson fracture (C1 burst) / Hangman's fracture (C2) / Clay-shoveler's fracture (C7 spinous process).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the classic plain-film appearance of an osteoporotic thoracic compression fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Anterior wedging with loss of anterior vertebral body height, usually with preserved endplate cortex and intact pedicles; often multiple levels, producing an increased thoracic kyphosis in an elderly patient.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the "winking owl" (absent pedicle) sign and what does it indicate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: On the AP thoracic film the paired pedicles look like an owl's eyes; destruction of one pedicle by tumour makes it disappear — a sign of metastatic/pathological bony destruction until proven otherwise.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which primary tumours most commonly metastasise to bone/spine?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Prostate, Breast, Lung, Kidney and Thyroid ("PBLKT"). Multiple myeloma also causes vertebral collapse and lytic lesions.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List key red flags in back pain suggesting sinister pathology.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Thoracic pain, age <20 or >55, night pain, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, neurological signs, saddle anaesthesia, and bladder/bowel dysfunction — raising concern for malignancy/MSCC or infection.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How is suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) managed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Urgent whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone, and immediate oncology/spinal referral — NOT reassurance from a plain film. A plain X-ray can be normal despite cord compression.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why does NICE advise against routine lumbar spine X-rays for non-specific low back pain?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: They deliver a significant gonadal radiation dose and very rarely change management. For suspected serious pathology (radiculopathy, cauda equina, infection, malignancy) MRI is the appropriate investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is spondylolysis and how does it appear radiographically?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A defect in the pars interarticularis. On oblique views it produces the "Scottie dog collar" sign (a break across the dog's neck), commonly at L5.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Define spondylolisthesis and how it is graded.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Forward slip of one vertebra on the one below (often L5 on S1). Graded I–IV by the Meyerding classification, based on the degree of slip in quartiles of the vertebral body width.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List the features of cauda equina syndrome and the correct management.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, faecal incontinence, and reduced anal tone. It is a surgical emergency requiring URGENT MRI and immediate spinal surgery referral — a plain X-ray must not delay the MRI.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What plain-film features suggest ankylosing spondylitis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Sacroiliitis, marginal syndesmophytes and a fused "bamboo spine". Suspect in a young man with inflammatory back pain (night pain, morning stiffness improving with activity).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a coccyx X-ray for suspected coccydynia/coccygeal fracture generally not recommended?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It rarely changes management — a coccygeal fracture is treated conservatively (analgesia, ring cushion, advice) whether or not it is seen — while delivering a significant pelvic and gonadal radiation dose. Coccydynia is largely a clinical diagnosis.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Who gets a sacral insufficiency fracture and why is the plain film often unhelpful?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Elderly/osteoporotic patients and those after pelvic radiotherapy. Fractures are frequently occult on plain film; they are best seen on MRI or CT, with the classic bilateral "Honda/H sign" of sacral ala uptake on bone scan.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What lines should you trace on an AP sacral radiograph, and what does disruption imply?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The arcuate lines — the smooth curved cortical lines running above each sacral foramen. A break or step in an arcuate line suggests a fracture through the sacral ala.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What plain-film features indicate sacroiliitis, and in which conditions?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Erosions, subchondral sclerosis and eventual ankylosis of the sacroiliac joints. Seen in ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which red-flag scenario makes a sacral fracture an emergency, and what must you check?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A sacral fracture as part of a high-energy pelvic ring injury may be unstable with haemorrhage and nerve injury (cauda equina/sacral plexus). Check perineal sensation and continence and obtain urgent orthopaedic/pelvic-trauma input.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why does a PA (rather than AP) chest film give an accurate cardiothoracic ratio?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: In PA the source is behind the patient and the film in front, so the anteriorly-placed heart lies close to the film and is magnified minimally. AP films magnify the heart and cannot be used to assess true cardiomegaly.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does the RIPE quality mnemonic stand for on a CXR?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Rotation (spinous processes equidistant between the medial clavicle ends), Inspiration (5–6 anterior or 8–10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm), Projection (PA vs AP), and Exposure/penetration (vertebrae just faintly visible behind the heart).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the silhouette sign and what does it tell you?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Loss of a normally sharp border localises adjacent pathology, because the abnormal tissue has the same density as the structure whose outline it effaces. A lost right heart border, for example, indicates right middle lobe pathology.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the upper limit of the normal cardiothoracic ratio on a PA film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Less than 50%. A ratio greater than 50% on a correctly-taken PA film indicates cardiomegaly.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which hemidiaphragm is normally higher, and what does costophrenic angle blunting suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (due to the liver). Blunting of a costophrenic angle suggests a pleural effusion.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why can't you diagnose cardiomegaly on an AP / portable chest film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The heart lies anteriorly and is far from the film, so the beam magnifies it. The cardiothoracic ratio is unreliable on AP — an apparently big heart may be normal. Confirm with a PA film or echo.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does a pleural effusion appear on a SUPINE film compared with an erect PA?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Instead of a meniscus with a blunted costophrenic angle, fluid layers posteriorly and produces a diffuse haziness or "veil" over the whole hemithorax, with lung vessels still visible through it — easily missed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the 'deep sulcus sign' and why does it matter on a supine film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: When supine, pneumothorax air collects anteriorly and basally rather than at the apex. It shows as an abnormally deep, lucent, sharply defined costophrenic angle — the key clue to a pneumothorax on a supine AP film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: State the correct radiographic positions for the ET tube and NG tube.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: ET tube: tip ~5 cm above the carina (mid-trachea). NG tube: must bisect the carina, pass below the left hemidiaphragm, and tip clearly within the stomach — never in the bronchi/lungs before feeding.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is confirming NG tube position before feeding a 'never event', and how is a tension pneumothorax diagnosed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: If feed is delivered through an NG tube whose tip is in the lungs it is fatal — so the tip must be confirmed below the diaphragm/in the stomach first. Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis; decompress immediately rather than waiting for an X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What view is the standard lateral chest radiograph, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A left lateral — the left side is placed against the film cassette. This minimises magnification of the heart (which sits on the left), giving a truer cardiac silhouette.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the 'spine sign' on a lateral chest X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Normally the thoracic vertebral bodies become progressively darker (more lucent) as the eye moves inferiorly. If the lower spine looks whiter/denser than the upper spine, suspect overlying lower lobe pathology (consolidation, collapse or effusion).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Loss of lucency in the retrosternal clear space suggests what?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: An anterior mediastinal mass — the 'terrible Ts': Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumour), (terrible) lymphoma/Lymphadenopathy, and retrosternal Thyroid. It warrants urgent work-up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why can a lateral detect a smaller pleural effusion than the PA?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The posterior costophrenic recess is the deepest, most dependent part of the pleural space. Fluid blunts this posterior costophrenic angle on the lateral before enough accumulates to blunt the lateral angle on the PA.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which hemidiaphragm cannot be traced along its whole length on the lateral, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The left hemidiaphragm — its anterior portion is obscured by the heart lying against it (silhouette sign). The right hemidiaphragm is visible throughout its length.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a small pneumothorax easier to see on an expiratory chest X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: On expiration lung volume falls but the pneumothorax volume stays constant, so the pneumothorax becomes relatively larger and stands out against a smaller, denser lung.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the CXR signs of a pneumothorax on an erect film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A visible thin white visceral pleural line with absent lung markings (lucent, black, avascular area) peripheral to it.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What sign suggests a pneumothorax on a supine chest X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The deep sulcus sign — an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle where anterior pleural air collects.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does an inhaled foreign body appear on an expiratory CXR in a child?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Ball-valve air trapping gives unilateral hyperinflation — the affected lung stays lucent (does not deflate) and the mediastinum shifts away from it on expiration.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How is a suspected tension pneumothorax diagnosed and managed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It is a clinical diagnosis (tracheal deviation away, hypotension, distended neck veins, hyperresonance, distress). Treat with immediate needle/finger decompression — do NOT wait for or request a CXR.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why are dedicated rib views usually NOT indicated for suspected simple rib fractures?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Confirming an uncomplicated fracture does not change management (analgesia, breathing exercises, conservative healing), rib fractures are frequently missed on plain film, and the important imaging job is a standard CXR to detect complications — not to count fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which complications of chest-wall trauma should you actively look for on the CXR?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Pneumothorax, haemothorax (blunted costophrenic angle/opacification), pulmonary contusion, and surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Define flail chest and its key clinical feature.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: 3 or more consecutive ribs each fractured in 2 or more places, producing a free segment that moves paradoxically. It is a clinical diagnosis, associated with underlying lung contusion and respiratory compromise.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does a fracture of the 1st/2nd rib or scapula imply, and what must you exclude?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: High-energy trauma — screen for great-vessel/aortic injury and brachial plexus damage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: In an infant, which rib fracture patterns are red flags for non-accidental injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Posterior rib fractures, and multiple rib fractures of differing ages — prompt a safeguarding referral.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is the sternum poorly seen on a standard frontal chest X-ray, and what views are used instead?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: On the PA/AP film the sternum overlies the dense vertebral column and mediastinum, so cortical detail is lost. Dedicated assessment uses a lateral sternum view (best for the body/manubrium) and an oblique/RAO view that rotates the sternum off the spine onto the cardiac shadow.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the classic mechanism of a sternal fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Blunt anterior chest trauma — classically the steering-wheel or seat-belt injury in a road-traffic collision, where the chest decelerates against the wheel/restraint. It is also seen after CPR.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a sternal fracture clinically important beyond the bone itself?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It is a marker of significant anterior chest trauma. The concern is the associated injuries: myocardial contusion/blunt cardiac injury, pericardial effusion/tamponade, great-vessel injury, pulmonary contusion and thoracic spine fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What investigations does a sternal fracture mandate to exclude blunt cardiac injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: An ECG and troponin, plus a period of cardiac monitoring, because of the risk of myocardial contusion and arrhythmia. CT chest is preferred in significant trauma as it images the sternum and associated injuries far better than plain film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List non-traumatic causes of sternal abnormality on imaging.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Metastasis, myeloma (lytic destruction), infection/osteomyelitis (classically post-sternotomy), and SAPHO syndrome (sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis/osteitis).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the three main indications for a supine abdominal X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Suspected bowel obstruction, suspected toxic megacolon in known colitis, and assessment of radio-opaque foreign bodies/calculi. It is NOT a routine test for abdominal pain — CT is far more useful.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: State the '3/6/9 rule' for upper limits of normal bowel diameter on AXR.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Small bowel >3 cm, large bowel >6 cm, and caecum >9 cm are all abnormally dilated.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you distinguish small from large bowel on an AXR?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Small bowel is central with valvulae conniventes (thin lines crossing the FULL width of the lumen); large bowel is peripheral with haustra (thicker lines that do NOT cross the full width).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Compare the radiographic appearance of sigmoid versus caecal volvulus.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Sigmoid volvulus: 'coffee bean'/inverted-U loop arising from the pelvis, pointing to the RUQ. Caecal volvulus: dilated caecum displaced to the LUQ in an 'embryo'/comma shape.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What proportion of gallstones and of renal calculi are radio-opaque on plain film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Only ~10% of gallstones are radio-opaque, whereas ~90% of renal/ureteric stones are — so a negative AXR does not exclude gallstones.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why does the erect position make air-fluid levels visible on an abdominal film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: With the patient upright and a horizontal X-ray beam, gas rises and fluid settles, so the flat gas–fluid interface (air-fluid level) becomes visible. A few short levels can be normal; multiple long levels in dilated loops suggest obstruction or ileus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the best plain radiograph for detecting free intraperitoneal air, and what is the classic sign?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The erect CHEST X-ray. Free gas rises and collects as a thin lucent crescent under the right hemidiaphragm. The erect AXR is largely abandoned for this; modern practice uses erect CXR + supine AXR, or CT.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is Rigler's sign?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The double-wall sign of pneumoperitoneum: free gas lies on BOTH sides of the bowel wall (inside the lumen and in the peritoneal cavity), making the bowel wall itself clearly visible. Seen on the supine film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you distinguish mechanical bowel obstruction from paralytic ileus radiologically?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Mechanical obstruction: dilated proximal loops with a collapsed distal bowel and empty rectum (a transition point). Paralytic ileus: generalised gas throughout small and large bowel, including the rectum, with no transition point.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the football sign?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A large oval lucency of free intraperitoneal gas outlining the whole peritoneal cavity, classically described in an infant/child with a massive pneumoperitoneum. It indicates a perforated viscus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the first-line investigation for suspected acute renal/ureteric colic, and why not a plain KUB?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Non-contrast CT KUB — it is far more sensitive, detects radiolucent stones, and shows size, site and obstruction. The plain KUB is NOT first-line for acute diagnosis; its main role is follow-up/surveillance of a known radio-opaque stone and post-lithotripsy monitoring.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which urinary stones are radiolucent (invisible on a plain KUB)?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Uric acid and indinavir stones are radiolucent. They are invisible on KUB but visible on CT. ~80–90% of calculi are radio-opaque (calcium oxalate/phosphate dense, struvite opaque, cystine only faintly opaque).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you distinguish a phlebolith from a ureteric stone on a KUB?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A phlebolith is a rounded pelvic venous calcification, often smooth with a lucent centre, lying below the ischial spines off the ureteric line. A ureteric stone is usually more irregular, dense throughout, and sits on the ureteric course (transverse process tips → sacroiliac joint → pelvic brim).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a staghorn calculus and what stone type causes it?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A large calculus that takes the shape of and fills the pelvicalyceal system. Usually struvite (infection/urease) stones. Radio-opaque and visible on KUB.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Describe the systematic 'line of the urinary tract' review on a KUB.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Renal outlines (calcification, staghorn, nephrocalcinosis) → line of the ureters over the tips of the transverse processes, across the sacroiliac joint and pelvic brim → bladder area in the lower pelvis for bladder stones.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why must you always look for a second injury on a pelvic X-ray?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The pelvis is a rigid bony ring, and a ring rarely breaks in only one place. A single displaced fracture implies a second fracture elsewhere in the ring, or disruption of the pubic symphysis or a sacroiliac joint.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is Shenton's line and what does a break in it indicate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A smooth continuous curve running from the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus along the inferomedial border of the femoral neck. A break or step suggests a femoral neck fracture or hip dislocation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How are neck of femur fractures classified and why does it matter?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Intracapsular (subcapital/transcervical) risks avascular necrosis and usually needs hemiarthroplasty/THR; extracapsular (intertrochanteric → DHS; subtrochanteric → IM nail) preserves the blood supply and can be fixed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which lines assess the acetabulum, and what is the normal pubic symphysis width?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The iliopectineal (anterior column) and ilioischial (posterior column) lines assess the acetabulum. The pubic symphysis should measure less than 5 mm.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What should you do if a hip fracture is clinically suspected but the X-ray is normal?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Obtain an MRI to exclude an occult fracture — a normal radiograph does not rule out a hip fracture in a patient who cannot weight-bear.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why can you never exclude a shoulder dislocation on a single AP radiograph?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The humeral head can appear seated on the AP while actually lying anterior or (classically) posterior to the glenoid. A second orthogonal view — scapular "Y" or axial/axillary — is required to confirm the head is truly reduced in the glenoid fossa.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Anterior glenohumeral dislocation: mechanism, radiographic position, and the two associated lesions.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Mechanism: abduction + external rotation. The head lies antero-inferiorly, medial to and below the coracoid ("sub-coracoid"). Associated: Hill-Sachs (postero-lateral humeral head impaction) and Bankart (antero-inferior glenoid labrum/bone) lesions.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation, and how do you assess it?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The axillary nerve. Test sensation over the "regimental badge" area of the lateral upper arm and assess deltoid function — document before and after reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Posterior shoulder dislocation: typical history and radiographic signs.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Classically follows a seizure or electrocution. AP shows the "light bulb" sign (head locked in internal rotation, appears rounded), loss of normal glenohumeral overlap, and a widened joint ("rim sign"). The axial/Y view is essential to confirm it — it is the classic missed diagnosis.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Name the common shoulder fractures and injuries to look for on a trauma shoulder X-ray.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Proximal humerus surgical neck fracture (Neer classification, common in elderly), greater tuberosity avulsion, clavicle fracture, and acromioclavicular joint separation. Also consider calcific tendinitis (non-traumatic rotator cuff calcification).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which third of the clavicle is most commonly fractured, and roughly what proportion of fractures does it account for?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The middle (mid-shaft) third — approximately 80% of clavicle fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: In a middle-third clavicle fracture, which way does each fragment displace and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The medial fragment is pulled UP by sternocleidomastoid; the lateral fragment is pulled DOWN by the weight of the arm.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the standard conservative management of an uncomplicated middle-third clavicle fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Broad arm sling and analgesia with early mobilisation as pain allows — most unite well without surgery.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What determines the stability of a lateral (distal) third clavicle fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Its relationship to the coracoclavicular ligaments — fractures with ligament disruption/displacement are unstable and more likely to require surgery.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List key indications for surgical fixation (ORIF) or urgent referral of a clavicle fracture.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Open fracture, skin tenting/threatened skin, neurovascular compromise, significant shortening or displacement, comminution, floating shoulder, and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which nerve is at risk in a surgical neck fracture of the humerus, and how does it present?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The axillary nerve — deltoid weakness (impaired abduction) and 'regimental badge' sensory loss over the lateral shoulder. This is the commonest osteoporotic humeral fracture in the elderly.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which nerve runs in the spiral/radial groove and is injured in a mid-shaft humeral fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The radial nerve — producing wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a Holstein-Lewis fracture and its complication?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft that characteristically entraps the radial nerve as it pierces the intermuscular septum.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which structures are at risk in a paediatric supracondylar fracture, and which radiographic signs help detect it?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The brachial artery and median nerve (especially the anterior interosseous nerve). Look for the fat pad/sail sign (effusion) and a disrupted anterior humeral line (should pass through the middle third of the capitellum).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What must be documented after every humeral fracture, and which finding is a surgical emergency?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A focused neurovascular exam. A supracondylar fracture with an absent radial pulse or signs of ischaemia is an emergency needing urgent reduction/orthopaedics to prevent compartment syndrome and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does a visible posterior fat pad on a lateral elbow X-ray indicate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It is ALWAYS abnormal — it signifies a joint effusion/haemarthrosis and therefore an occult fracture until proven otherwise, managed as a fracture even if no line is seen.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: A raised fat pad sign in an ADULT vs a CHILD suggests which fractures?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Adult → radial head fracture (commonest occult adult elbow fracture, FOOSH). Child → supracondylar fracture (commonest paediatric elbow fracture).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Where should the anterior humeral line pass, and what does displacement mean?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Down the anterior humeral cortex through the MIDDLE THIRD of the capitellum. If it passes through the anterior third/in front, suspect a posteriorly displaced supracondylar fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the radiocapitellar line and what does an abnormal one mean?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A line through the radial neck should point to the CENTRE of the capitellum in ALL views. If it misses, there is a radial head dislocation (look for an ulnar fracture — Monteggia).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the CRITOE order and its clinical trap?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Capitellum, Radial head, Internal (medial) epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External (lateral) epicondyle. The medial epicondyle must appear BEFORE the trochlea — a 'trochlea' without a medial epicondyle = an avulsed medial epicondyle in the joint.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why must a forearm X-ray always include BOTH the elbow and wrist?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The radius and ulna form a rigid bony ring linked by the proximal and distal radioulnar joints. A single displaced/angulated shaft fracture is frequently accompanied by a dislocation at the other end (Monteggia/Galeazzi), which will be missed if only one joint is imaged.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Define a Monteggia fracture-dislocation and the key radiographic check.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Fracture of the PROXIMAL ULNA with DISLOCATION of the RADIAL HEAD. Check the radiocapitellar line: a line along the radial neck should pass through the centre of the capitellum on every view; if it misses, the radial head is dislocated. Usually needs ORIF in adults.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Define a Galeazzi fracture-dislocation and the key radiographic check.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Fracture of the DISTAL RADIUS with dislocation/subluxation of the DISTAL RADIOULNAR JOINT (DRUJ). Look for DRUJ widening, ulnar styloid avulsion or a prominent ulnar head on the lateral. Usually needs ORIF in adults.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What does the mnemonic MUGR stand for?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Monteggia = Ulna (proximal ulnar fracture + radial head dislocation); Galeazzi = Radius (distal radial fracture + DRUJ dislocation). Alternatively GRUM. It tells you which bone is fractured in each named fracture-dislocation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the limb-threatening red flag in any forearm fracture, and how is it detected and treated?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Compartment syndrome. Earliest signs are pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the fingers (pulselessness/paraesthesia are late). It is a surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy; always document distal neurovascular status.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Colles' fracture: displacement direction and eponymous deformity?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Extra-articular distal radius fracture with DORSAL displacement/angulation, giving the “dinner fork” deformity. Classically a FOOSH in an osteoporotic elderly woman; the normal ~11° volar tilt is reversed to dorsal tilt.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does Smith's fracture differ from Colles'?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Smith's is the “reverse Colles” — VOLAR (palmar) displacement of the distal radius fragment (“garden spade” deformity), typically from a fall onto a flexed wrist. Barton's, by contrast, is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Normal distal radius parameters on plain film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Radial height ~11 mm, radial inclination ~22° (PA), and volar/palmar tilt ~11° (lateral). Loss of height/inclination or reversal to dorsal tilt indicates a displaced fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Lateral wrist: how do you distinguish lunate from perilunate dislocation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Draw the radius–lunate–capitate line. LUNATE dislocation: lunate tips volar off the radius (“spilled teacup”). PERILUNATE dislocation: lunate stays aligned with the radius but the capitate dislocates dorsally off the lunate. Both are orthopaedic emergencies.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the Terry-Thomas sign and what does it indicate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A scapholunate gap >3 mm on the PA wrist film (widened space between scaphoid and lunate). It indicates scapholunate dissociation and is associated with disruption of Gilula's carpal arcs.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What clinical sign is most sensitive for a scaphoid fracture, and what is the classic mechanism?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox (also scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on thumb telescoping). Classic mechanism: fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why do waist and proximal pole scaphoid fractures risk avascular necrosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply — the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the distal pole and perfuses distal-to-proximal. A waist or proximal pole fracture cuts off inflow to the proximal fragment, causing AVN and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you manage a clinically suspected scaphoid fracture when the initial X-ray is normal?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Treat as a fracture: immobilise in a scaphoid/futuro splint (thumb spica) and re-assess in ~10–14 days with a repeat X-ray, or proceed to MRI (most sensitive, increasingly first-line) or CT to confirm/exclude. Never simply discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What views make up a dedicated scaphoid series and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Four views: PA, PA with ulnar deviation (elongates the scaphoid), oblique, and lateral. They profile the scaphoid so a subtle fracture line is not foreshortened — but the fracture is still frequently occult on the initial film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is SNAC wrist and how does undisplaced vs displaced fracture management differ?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: SNAC = Scaphoid Non-union Advanced Collapse, secondary wrist osteoarthritis from a missed/non-united fracture. Undisplaced waist fractures are cast; displaced or proximal pole fractures often need surgical fixation (e.g. Herbert screw).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a boxer's fracture and which deformity must you assess clinically?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Fracture of the 5th (± 4th) metacarpal neck from punching, with volar angulation of the distal fragment. Angulation is measured on the lateral, but rotational deformity is assessed clinically (fingers should point to the scaphoid on flexion) and mandates correction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Distinguish Bennett's from Rolando's fracture.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Both are intra-articular fractures at the base of the 1st metacarpal (thumb). Bennett's is a two-part fracture-dislocation (unstable; abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally/radially). Rolando's is a comminuted Y- or T-shaped version with a worse prognosis. Both need hand-surgery review.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is mallet finger and how does it appear?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Bony (or tendinous) avulsion of the extensor tendon at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx, causing a drooped DIP joint that cannot actively extend. Look for a small dorsal avulsion flake on the lateral view.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a volar plate avulsion injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A small avulsion fracture at the volar (palmar) base of the middle phalanx following hyperextension at the PIP joint. Best seen as a tiny flake on the lateral radiograph.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a 'fight bite' and why is it dangerous?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A clenched-fist injury: a laceration over the MCP joint sustained by punching someone's teeth. It is a human-bite wound that inoculates the joint/tendon sheath with oral flora, risking septic arthritis and tenosynovitis. Requires washout and antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) and must never be closed primarily.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department after a fall with loss of consciousness, vomiting, and a GCS of 13. What is the most appropriate imaging investigation to detect intracranial injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT head
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: NICE head injury guidance triages patients with concerning features (reduced GCS, vomiting, LOC risk factors) to CT head, which detects intracranial haemorrhage and injury. A skull X-ray is not used to make this decision, and a normal film would not exclude brain injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skull X-ray in an elderly patient shows multiple small, well-defined lytic "punched-out" lesions throughout the vault. Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Multiple myeloma
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Multiple well-defined lytic "punched-out" lesions are the classic skull appearance of multiple myeloma. Paget's gives "cotton wool" sclerosis, hyperparathyroidism a granular "pepperpot" skull, and thalassaemia a "hair-on-end" pattern.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skull X-ray is requested as part of the assessment of a 6-month-old infant with unexplained bruising and a suspicious limb fracture. What is the primary reason the skull film is being taken here?
options: As part of a skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury
To assess the sella turcica for a pituitary tumour
To confirm the child is safe for discharge
To detect a ventriculoperitoneal shunt blockage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: As part of a skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In suspected non-accidental injury the skull is imaged as part of a full paediatric skeletal survey looking for occult fractures. Intracranial injury would be assessed with CT/MRI, and safeguarding referral is mandatory. The skull film cannot clear a child for discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old is assaulted and has left facial swelling. The OM radiograph shows a soft-tissue "teardrop" projecting from the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum, with opacification of the sinus. He reports double vision on looking up. Which fracture is most likely?
options: Orbital blowout fracture of the floor
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Orbital blowout fracture of the floor
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The teardrop sign (herniated orbital contents in the antral roof), antral opacification and diplopia on upgaze from inferior rectus tethering are classic for an orbital floor blowout fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: When reviewing a facial X-ray using McGrigor–Campbell lines, which structures does line 2 cross?
options: Zygomatico-frontal sutures and superior orbital margins
Zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra
Mandibular condyles and the occlusal line
Nasal bones and anterior nasal spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Line 1 runs across the zygomatico-frontal sutures/superior orbital margins, line 2 across the zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra, and line 3 across the mandibular condyles and occlusal line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with facial trauma has a tense, proptosed, painful eye and rapidly falling visual acuity after their injury. What is the most important immediate concern?
options: Le Fort I fracture with malocclusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Retrobulbar haemorrhage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A tense, proptosed, painful eye with falling acuity after trauma indicates retrobulbar haemorrhage, a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate orbital decompression, not further plain imaging.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old is punched in the nose. There is swelling and mild deviation but no epistaxis now, no CSF leak, and no other injury. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Request lateral nasal and OM X-rays to confirm the fracture
Arrange an urgent CT of the facial bones
Examine inside the nose, then plan clinical review at 5–7 days
Immediately manipulate the nasal bones under anaesthesia
Discharge with no examination as nasal fractures are trivial
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Examine inside the nose, then plan clinical review at 5–7 days
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A simple nasal fracture is a clinical diagnosis and X-ray does not change management. You must examine the septum for a haematoma, then review at 5–7 days once swelling settles to assess deformity. CT is reserved for suspected skull base injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On examining a patient after nasal trauma you find a boggy, bilateral swelling on the nasal septum. What is the correct action?
options: Prescribe oral antibiotics alone and discharge
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent incision and drainage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a septal haematoma — the must-not-miss injury. Untreated it causes septal cartilage necrosis/abscess and saddle-nose deformity, so it requires urgent incision and drainage, not delay or imaging.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with facial trauma has clear fluid dripping from one nostril that forms a 'halo/tramline' sign on tissue. Which statement is correct?
options: A nasal X-ray will confirm the diagnosis
This indicates a septal haematoma requiring drainage
Beta-2-transferrin testing and CT with neurosurgical input are indicated
It is expected after any nasal fracture and needs no action
Manipulation of the nasal bones should be performed urgently
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Beta-2-transferrin testing and CT with neurosurgical input are indicated
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Clear rhinorrhoea with a halo/tramline sign suggests CSF leak from a cribriform plate/anterior skull base fracture. It is confirmed with beta-2-transferrin and imaged with CT, with neurosurgical involvement — a nasal X-ray has no role.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old is assaulted and has a fracture of the right mandibular body confirmed on OPG. What is the single most important next step in interpreting the film?
options: Conclude the assessment as one fracture is identified
Deliberately search for a second (often contralateral) fracture
Request an urgent CT head for intracranial injury
Measure the degree of dental caries present
Assess the maxillary sinuses for a fluid level
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Deliberately search for a second (often contralateral) fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The mandible is a bony ring, so fractures are frequently in two places. A right body fracture classically pairs with a contralateral condylar or angle fracture — missing the second fracture is a common exam and clinical trap.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which mandibular fracture pattern is most likely to compromise the airway?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Bilateral anterior (parasymphyseal, 'bucket-handle') fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A bilateral anterior fracture frees the central fragment; the tongue attached to it can fall backwards and obstruct the airway — a true emergency requiring immediate airway management.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised sign of a mandibular fracture on imaging or examination?
options: A lucent line crossing the cortex
A step in the lower-border cortex
A tooth lying within the fracture line
Uniform widening of the periodontal ligament of all teeth
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Uniform widening of the periodontal ligament of all teeth
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Fracture signs are a lucent line, a cortical step (especially at the lower border), malocclusion, and a tooth in the fracture line. Generalised uniform periodontal ligament widening is not a fracture sign.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 3-year-old presents drooling, toxic and sitting forward with muffled voice and rapidly worsening stridor. A junior colleague suggests obtaining a lateral soft tissue neck X-ray to look for the thumbprint sign. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Send the child to the X-ray department for a lateral neck film
Lie the child flat and examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Keep the child calm and upright and summon senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway
Give oral antibiotics and reassess in one hour
Perform flexible nasendoscopy at the bedside without preparation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Keep the child calm and upright and summon senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is suspected epiglottitis — an airway emergency. Do not distress the child, examine the throat, lie them flat, or send for imaging, as any of these may precipitate complete airway obstruction. The priority is a secured airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support before any investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a correctly performed lateral soft tissue neck radiograph, which finding best supports a diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess?
options: Prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body, possibly with gas or an air-fluid level
A radiolucent fish bone in the vallecula
Narrowing of the piriform fossae bilaterally
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body, possibly with gas or an air-fluid level
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess widens the prevertebral soft tissues (rough rule >~7 mm at C2, >~14–22 mm at C6), sometimes with gas or an air-fluid level, and the child holds the neck extended. The steeple sign is croup (and a frontal-view sign), the swollen epiglottis is epiglottitis, and radiolucent bones are not seen on plain film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A lateral neck film reported as showing 'widened prevertebral soft tissues' was taken while the child was crying with the neck flexed. Before referring for suspected retropharyngeal abscess, what is the most important next step?
options: Immediately drain the collection in the emergency department
Repeat the film in inspiration with the neck extended
Request an urgent CT with contrast without any further plain films
Reassure and discharge as the finding is always artefactual
Start intravenous steroids for presumed croup
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Repeat the film in inspiration with the neck extended
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Flexion and expiration falsely widen the prevertebral soft tissues and are a classic pitfall. A film taken in inspiration with the neck extended should be obtained to confirm genuine widening before escalating. The apparent swelling may resolve on a correctly performed film, avoiding unnecessary intervention.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a high-speed motorbike crash with midline cervical tenderness and paraesthesiae in both hands. What is the most appropriate cervical spine imaging?
options: No imaging — apply NEXUS and discharge
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT cervical spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is significant trauma with high-risk features (dangerous mechanism, paraesthesiae). NICE/modern practice favours CT over plain films because plain films miss injuries. The Canadian C-Spine Rule mandates imaging here, and CT is the correct modality.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A junior doctor reports a 'normal' lateral cervical spine film in a trauma patient, but the image only shows down to C6. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Clear the cervical spine and remove the collar
Accept the film as adequate and discharge
Regard the film as inadequate and obtain further imaging (e.g. CT) while keeping the neck immobilised
Repeat the same lateral view once more only
Reassure the patient and arrange outpatient MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Regard the film as inadequate and obtain further imaging (e.g. CT) while keeping the neck immobilised
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An adequate lateral must show C1 to the C7/T1 junction. Injuries at the cervicothoracic junction are commonly missed. You cannot clear a c-spine on an inadequate film — keep it immobilised and image further, typically with CT.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On an open-mouth (peg) view, the lateral masses of C1 are splayed laterally beyond the margins of C2 following an axial-loading injury. Which fracture does this suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Jefferson (C1 burst) fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the C1 ring from axial loading. On the peg/open-mouth view the C1 lateral masses are displaced outward (overhang) relative to C2, which is the classic sign.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which single finding on a lateral cervical radiograph is a soft-tissue clue to an occult underlying fracture?
options: Preservation of the normal cervical lordosis
Symmetrical C1 lateral masses on the peg view
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Prevertebral soft tissue widening
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Prevertebral soft tissue widening reflects blood/oedema anterior to the vertebrae and can be the only clue to an occult fracture. The other options are all normal/reassuring findings.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 78-year-old woman presents with sudden mid-back pain after bending down. AP and lateral thoracic radiographs show anterior wedging of a mid-thoracic vertebral body with loss of anterior height, preserved endplate cortex and two intact symmetric pedicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Osteoporotic wedge compression fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Anterior wedging with preserved endplate cortex and intact pedicles in an elderly patient after minor trauma is the classic picture of a benign osteoporotic compression fracture. Pedicle destruction or an unusual level would raise concern for a pathological/metastatic cause.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On an AP thoracic spine radiograph, one vertebra is noted to have only a single visible pedicle, with the other pedicle absent. What does this "winking owl" sign most strongly suggest?
options: Metastatic destruction of the pedicle by tumour
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Metastatic destruction of the pedicle by tumour
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The paired pedicles resemble an owl's eyes on the AP view; loss of one (the winking owl / absent pedicle sign) reflects bony destruction, classically metastatic tumour, and warrants urgent further imaging and investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 60-year-old man with known prostate cancer reports 3 weeks of thoracic back pain, worse at night, with new lower-limb weakness and difficulty passing urine. His thoracic spine X-ray appears unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent whole-spine MRI with dexamethasone and specialist referral
Reassure and discharge as the film is normal
Prescribe simple analgesia and review in 6 weeks
Repeat the plain film in 2 weeks
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent whole-spine MRI with dexamethasone and specialist referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Red flags (cancer history, night pain, neurology, bladder dysfunction) point to metastatic spinal cord compression. A normal plain film does not exclude it; management is urgent whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone and oncology/spinal referral, never reassurance from an X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old man presents with 8 weeks of non-specific low back pain, no red flag features and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate imaging?
options: AP and lateral lumbosacral spine X-ray
No imaging — reassure and manage conservatively
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: No imaging — reassure and manage conservatively
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: NICE advises against routine imaging for non-specific low back pain without red flags. Plain films carry a significant gonadal dose and rarely change management; MRI is reserved for suspected serious pathology. Management is reassurance, activity advice, analgesia and safety-netting.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with acute bilateral leg pain, saddle numbness, and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows reduced anal tone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request AP and lateral lumbosacral radiographs
Arrange urgent MRI of the spine and refer to spinal surgery
Prescribe analgesia and review in 2 weeks
Request a CT lumbar spine as first-line
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Arrange urgent MRI of the spine and refer to spinal surgery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: These features indicate cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Urgent MRI and immediate spinal surgery referral are required. A plain X-ray is useless and must not delay definitive imaging and decompression.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An oblique lumbar spine radiograph shows a "collar" across the neck of the Scottie dog at L5. Which abnormality does this represent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The neck of the Scottie dog corresponds to the pars interarticularis; a break or "collar" across it indicates spondylolysis. If bilateral, this can permit a forward slip (spondylolisthesis), but the collar sign itself denotes the pars defect.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old woman attends A&E with isolated coccygeal pain after slipping and landing on her buttocks. She is neurologically intact with focal tenderness over the coccyx. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Request an AP and lateral coccyx X-ray to confirm a fracture before treating
Arrange urgent MRI of the sacrum and coccyx
Reassure, provide analgesia and a ring cushion, and advise on activity modification without imaging
Refer for CT of the pelvis to exclude a pelvic ring injury
Admit for orthopaedic surgical fixation of the coccyx
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Reassure, provide analgesia and a ring cushion, and advise on activity modification without imaging
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Coccydynia is largely a clinical diagnosis and a coccygeal fracture is managed conservatively regardless of X-ray findings. A coccyx film therefore rarely changes management and cannot justify its pelvic/gonadal radiation dose. There is no high-energy mechanism or neurological deficit to warrant CT/MRI or surgery.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis develops progressive low sacral/buttock pain over two weeks with no injury. A plain sacral radiograph is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that the normal film excludes a fracture
Prescribe a coccyx ring cushion and discharge
Request a repeat plain film in six weeks
Start empirical antibiotics for suspected osteomyelitis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Arrange MRI of the sacrum
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: New sacral pain in an elderly osteoporotic patient should raise suspicion of a sacral insufficiency fracture (or metastasis). These are frequently occult on plain film, so a normal radiograph does not exclude them; MRI is the sensitive investigation of choice.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 26-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle collision. He has posterior pelvic pain and a sacral fracture is suspected as part of a pelvic ring injury. Which assessment is most important to perform urgently?
options: Measurement of coccygeal angulation on a lateral film
Assessment of perineal sensation and continence
Range of movement at both hips
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Assessment of perineal sensation and continence
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A sacral fracture within a high-energy pelvic ring injury may be unstable and can injure the cauda equina or sacral plexus. Assessing perineal (saddle) sensation and continence screens for this neurological injury and, together with concern for haemorrhage, mandates urgent orthopaedic/pelvic-trauma input.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A chest radiograph shows the medial ends of the clavicles unequally spaced from the spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae. Which aspect of image quality is inadequate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Rotation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Adequate rotation is confirmed when the spinous processes lie equidistant between the medial ends of the clavicles. Unequal spacing means the patient is rotated, which distorts mediastinal and cardiac contours and can mimic or mask pathology.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient's PA chest film shows loss of the right heart border with adjacent air-space opacification. Which lobe is most likely affected?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Right middle lobe
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: By the silhouette sign, loss of the right heart border indicates pathology in the anatomically adjacent right middle lobe. Right lower lobe consolidation instead effaces the right hemidiaphragm, not the heart border.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young man presents with sudden breathlessness, hypotension, a trachea deviated to the left, and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Request an urgent portable chest X-ray before treating
Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
Insert a formal intercostal chest drain after imaging
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis. Treatment must not be delayed for imaging; immediate decompression (needle then chest drain) is life-saving. Waiting for a CXR risks fatal cardiovascular collapse.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a PA chest radiograph, which finding most specifically suggests a perforated abdominal viscus?
options: A meniscus at the lung base
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Free air under the diaphragm
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free gas beneath the hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect film indicates a perforated viscus and mandates urgent surgical review. Costophrenic blunting and a meniscus indicate effusion; hilar enlargement suggests lymphadenopathy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: When assessing inspiration quality on a PA chest film, how many posterior ribs should be visible above the diaphragm in an adequate film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Adequate inspiration is shown by 8–10 posterior ribs (or 5–6 anterior ribs) visible above the diaphragm. A poorer inspiratory effort crowds the basal lung markings and can mimic consolidation or cardiomegaly.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 72-year-old ICU patient has an AP portable supine chest film. The cardiac silhouette looks enlarged with a cardiothoracic ratio well above 50%. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Report definite cardiomegaly and start diuresis
Apparent cardiomegaly is unreliable on an AP film due to magnification; correlate with a PA film or echo
Conclude the film is technically inadequate and cannot be reported at all
Report biventricular failure on the basis of heart size
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Apparent cardiomegaly is unreliable on an AP film due to magnification; correlate with a PA film or echo
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On an AP projection the heart lies further from the film and is magnified, so the cardiothoracic ratio cannot be used to diagnose cardiomegaly. The correct response is to note apparent enlargement is unreliable and correlate with a PA film or echocardiography, not to act on the measurement.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A nurse asks you to confirm an NG tube is safe for feeding on a portable chest X-ray. Which single finding confirms correct placement?
options: The tube tip lies at the level of the carina
The tube deviates to the right at the level of the aortic arch
The tube bisects the carina, passes below the left hemidiaphragm and the tip is in the stomach
The tube tip is seen in the right lower zone
The tube follows the line of a bronchus
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The tube bisects the carina, passes below the left hemidiaphragm and the tip is in the stomach
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Safe NG placement requires the tube to bisect the carina, remain midline, cross below the left hemidiaphragm and have its tip clearly within the stomach. Feeding through a tube whose tip is in the lungs is a fatal never event, so any bronchial course must be excluded before feed is given.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A ventilated patient in resus has a supine AP film. There is an abnormally deep, lucent, sharply outlined right costophrenic angle but no obvious apical lung edge. What does this most likely represent?
options: A pneumothorax shown by the deep sulcus sign
Free gas under the diaphragm from a perforation
Consolidation of the right lower lobe
Normal appearance for a supine film
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A pneumothorax shown by the deep sulcus sign
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: When a patient is supine, pneumothorax air rises to the anterior and basal chest rather than the apex, so the usual apical lung edge is absent. The deep sulcus sign — an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle — is the key clue to a pneumothorax on a supine AP film. A layering effusion causes diffuse haziness, not a lucent sulcus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A PA chest film shows a subtle opacity that seems to lie behind the cardiac shadow. A lateral is obtained to localise it. Which structures on the lateral are used to assign a lesion to a specific lobe?
options: The aortic knuckle and the azygos vein
The oblique (major) fissures, plus the horizontal (minor) fissure on the right
The costophrenic angles and the gastric bubble
The tracheal air column and carina
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The oblique (major) fissures, plus the horizontal (minor) fissure on the right
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The obliquely running major fissures divide upper/middle from lower lobes; the right horizontal fissure separates right upper from right middle lobe. Relating the lesion to these fissures on the lateral assigns it to a lobe in the antero-posterior plane that the PA cannot resolve.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a lateral chest radiograph you notice the lower thoracic vertebral bodies appear whiter (denser) than the upper ones. What does this 'spine sign' most suggest?
options: Lower lobe pathology such as consolidation, collapse or effusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Lower lobe pathology such as consolidation, collapse or effusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Normally the vertebrae become progressively more lucent (darker) inferiorly as soft tissue thins out. Increasing density towards the lower spine (a positive spine sign) indicates superimposed lower lobe pathology projected over the vertebral column.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young adult's lateral chest film shows loss of the normal lucency in the retrosternal clear space. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate concern and next step?
options: A small anterior pneumothorax; discharge with advice
An anterior mediastinal mass (e.g. lymphoma/thymoma); arrange CT for urgent characterisation
Left lower lobe collapse; repeat the PA in one week
A normal thymic remnant; no further action
A large pleural effusion; therapeutic aspiration on the ward
