investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: An anterior mediastinal mass (e.g. lymphoma/thymoma); arrange CT for urgent characterisation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The retrosternal clear space is normally lucent; filling it in (increased whiteness) points to an anterior mediastinal mass — the 'terrible Ts'. In a young adult lymphoma is a key concern, and a mass here can threaten the airway or SVC, so urgent cross-sectional imaging with CT is warranted.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has a suspected small apical pneumothorax not clearly seen on the inspiratory film. Why can an expiratory film help?
options: The pneumothorax expands as the patient breathes out
Lung volume falls while the pneumothorax volume stays constant, making it relatively larger and more conspicuous
Expiration increases pleural air pressure and enlarges the pneumothorax
The heart moves and uncovers the apex
Expiration reduces the density of the lung, making air easier to see
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Lung volume falls while the pneumothorax volume stays constant, making it relatively larger and more conspicuous
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On expiration the lung deflates but the trapped pleural air does not, so the pneumothorax occupies a proportionally larger fraction of a smaller, denser hemithorax and becomes easier to detect. Note that BTS guidance regards routine expiratory films as adding little over a good inspiratory film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 3-year-old presents after a choking episode. An expiratory CXR is requested for suspected inhaled foreign body. Which finding best supports the diagnosis?
options: The affected lung deflates more than the normal lung
Unilateral hyperinflation with the affected lung staying lucent and the mediastinum shifting away on expiration
A visible visceral pleural line at the apex
Complete white-out of the affected hemithorax
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Unilateral hyperinflation with the affected lung staying lucent and the mediastinum shifting away on expiration
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A ball-valve foreign body lets air in but not out, so the obstructed lung cannot deflate on expiration. It stays lucent while the normal lung empties, and the mediastinum shifts away from the affected side — the contrast is greatest on the expiratory film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A trauma patient is hypotensive with a deviated trachea, distended neck veins and a hyperresonant, silent right chest. What is the correct next step?
options: Request an urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm
Observe on high-flow oxygen and repeat imaging
Insert a formal chest drain after the X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immediate needle or finger decompression
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis and immediate life threat. Treatment must not be delayed by imaging: perform emergency needle/finger decompression at once, then a definitive chest drain. You do NOT wait for or request a chest X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old man attends after falling against a bannister. He is comfortable, saturating 98% on air, with focal tenderness over a left lateral rib. Chest is clear on auscultation. What is the most appropriate imaging approach?
options: Dedicated left rib views to confirm and count the fractures
Standard erect chest X-ray to exclude complications
CT chest to grade the fracture
No imaging is ever needed in chest trauma
Repeat rib views in 10 days to check healing
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Standard erect chest X-ray to exclude complications
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Dedicated rib views do not change management of a simple fracture and miss fractures anyway. The value of imaging is a standard CXR to detect pneumothorax, haemothorax, contusion or surgical emphysema.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which finding best defines flail chest?
options: A single rib fractured in two places
Two adjacent ribs each fractured once
Three or more consecutive ribs each fractured in two or more places
Any fracture of the first rib
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Three or more consecutive ribs each fractured in two or more places
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This frees a chest-wall segment that moves paradoxically. It is a clinical diagnosis associated with underlying lung contusion and respiratory compromise, and may need ventilatory support.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A cyclist hit by a car has a fractured left 10th and 11th rib. Beyond analgesia, what is the priority concern?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Splenic and renal injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Lower rib fractures (9–12) overlie solid organs: left-sided fractures risk splenic injury and either side risks renal injury (right-sided risk liver). Assess with CT/FAST for intra-abdominal injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old is brought in after a high-speed RTC in which his chest struck the steering wheel. A lateral sternum view shows a cortical step in the sternal body. He is haemodynamically stable. Which is the single most important immediate investigation to exclude a dangerous associated injury?
options: Repeat plain sternal radiograph in 24 hours
12-lead ECG and troponin with cardiac monitoring
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: 12-lead ECG and troponin with cardiac monitoring
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A sternal fracture is a marker of significant anterior chest trauma. The key concern is blunt cardiac injury (myocardial contusion) with its arrhythmia risk, so an ECG, troponin and a period of cardiac monitoring are mandated. The other options address non-traumatic or non-urgent issues.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: In a patient with significant blunt anterior chest trauma and a suspected sternal fracture, why is CT chest generally preferred over dedicated plain sternal views?
options: CT uses a lower radiation dose than plain film
CT images the sternum and the associated cardiac, vascular, pulmonary and spinal injuries far better
Plain film cannot show any bony fracture
CT is the only test that can diagnose myeloma
Plain film requires the patient to be prone, which is impossible in trauma
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT images the sternum and the associated cardiac, vascular, pulmonary and spinal injuries far better
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: CT is superior for the sternum itself and, crucially, for the associated injuries that actually matter — myocardial contusion, pericardial effusion, great-vessel injury, pulmonary contusion and thoracic spine fracture — so in significant trauma it is preferred over plain radiography.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a sternal fracture is found to have a concomitant fracture elsewhere that is easily missed. Which structure should be specifically evaluated because it forms a bony ring with the sternum?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Thoracic spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The sternum, ribs and thoracic spine form a ring, so a fracture in the sternum should prompt a deliberate search for a concomitant thoracic spine fracture, which is frequently overlooked.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 78-year-old with chronic constipation has a supine AXR showing a large inverted-U ('coffee bean') gas-filled loop arising from the pelvis and projecting towards the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Sigmoid volvulus
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A coffee-bean/inverted-U loop rising out of the pelvis and pointing to the RUQ is the classic sigmoid volvulus. Caecal volvulus instead displaces the caecum to the LUQ ('embryo'/comma shape). It is the commonest volvulus and typically affects elderly, constipated patients.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a flare of ulcerative colitis is febrile and tachycardic. The supine AXR shows a transverse colon dilated to 7 cm with mucosal islands and loss of haustra. What is the immediate concern?
options: Toxic megacolon with risk of perforation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Toxic megacolon with risk of perforation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A transverse colon >6 cm with mucosal islands/thumbprinting, loss of haustra and systemic toxicity in a colitic patient is toxic megacolon — a medical emergency that risks perforation and needs urgent surgical and gastroenterology review.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A registrar suspects a bowel perforation. Which single investigation is best for demonstrating free intraperitoneal air?
options: Lateral decubitus abdominal film in the dark
Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Erect chest X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free intraperitoneal air is best seen as air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. The supine AXR is poor at demonstrating free air, so it is not the correct film when perforation is suspected (CT is definitive).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a supine AXR, which feature best identifies a dilated loop as SMALL bowel rather than large bowel?
options: Haustra that do not cross the full lumen
Valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the lumen
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the lumen
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Small bowel lies centrally and shows valvulae conniventes — closely spaced lines that cross the ENTIRE width of the lumen. Large bowel is peripheral with haustra that only project partway across. The relevant small-bowel dilatation threshold is >3 cm, not >6 cm.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about calcified structures on a plain AXR is correct?
options: Only about 10% of renal calculi are radio-opaque
About 90% of renal/ureteric calculi are radio-opaque
Vascular calcification never appears on plain films
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: About 90% of renal/ureteric calculi are radio-opaque
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Roughly 90% of renal/ureteric stones are radio-opaque and may be seen on AXR, whereas only about 10% of gallstones are radio-opaque, so a normal AXR does not exclude gallstones. Pancreatic and vascular (e.g. aortic) calcification are also common incidental findings.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 68-year-old with sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen is suspected of having a perforated peptic ulcer. Which single plain radiograph is most sensitive for detecting free intraperitoneal gas?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Erect (upright) chest X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On an erect CXR free gas rises to sit beneath the diaphragm, giving a thin lucent crescent under the right hemidiaphragm, and even small volumes are detectable. The routine erect AXR adds little and is largely abandoned; CT is used when plain films are equivocal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An erect abdominal film shows multiple long air-fluid levels in centrally placed dilated loops with valvulae conniventes crossing the full bowel width, while the rectum is empty of gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Small-bowel obstruction
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Central dilated loops (>3 cm) with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width, multiple air-fluid levels, and a collapsed distal bowel/empty rectum indicate mechanical small-bowel obstruction. Ileus would show generalised gas including the rectum with no transition point.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A supine abdominal film shows the bowel wall outlined by gas on both its luminal and peritoneal sides, making the wall itself clearly visible. What does this represent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Rigler's (double-wall) sign of pneumoperitoneum
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of the bowel wall, seen with free intraperitoneal gas, and indicates a perforated viscus — a surgical emergency requiring resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review, not merely a radiological curiosity.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old presents with acute left-sided loin-to-groin colic and microscopic haematuria. What is the single most appropriate first-line imaging investigation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Non-contrast CT KUB
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: CT KUB is the investigation of choice for acute renal/ureteric colic: it is highly sensitive, detects radiolucent stones, and defines size, site and obstruction. A plain KUB is not first-line for acute diagnosis — its role is follow-up of a known opaque stone.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with recurrent stones has a normal plain KUB despite classic colic. Which stone composition best explains a stone that is invisible on the plain film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Uric acid
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Uric acid (and indinavir) stones are radiolucent and invisible on KUB, though visible on CT. Calcium oxalate/phosphate and struvite are radio-opaque; cystine is only faintly opaque but still usually visible.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A KUB shows a rounded calcific density in the pelvis with a lucent centre, lying below the ischial spines and off the expected ureteric line. What is this most likely to be?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Phlebolith
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Phleboliths are rounded pelvic venous calcifications, typically smooth with a lucent centre and sited below the ischial spines away from the ureteric course — a classic mimic of a distal ureteric stone, which is usually irregular, dense and on the ureteric line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a known obstructing ureteric stone develops a fever of 39°C, rigors and hydronephrosis on imaging. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Discharge with oral antibiotics and follow-up KUB
Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) plus IV antibiotics
Watchful waiting for spontaneous stone passage
Oral analgesia and repeat plain KUB in 48 hours
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) plus IV antibiotics
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An obstructing, infected stone (pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency. It requires urgent drainage of the obstructed, infected system by nephrostomy or stent together with IV antibiotics and resuscitation; definitive stone treatment (e.g. lithotripsy) is deferred.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls and presents with a shortened, externally rotated left leg. The AP pelvis shows a break in Shenton's line at the femoral neck with the fracture line above the intertrochanteric region. Which classification and typical management is correct?
options: Intracapsular subcapital — high AVN risk, hemiarthroplasty/THR
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intracapsular subcapital — high AVN risk, hemiarthroplasty/THR
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A fracture at the femoral neck above the trochanters is intracapsular. This disrupts the retinacular blood supply to the femoral head, carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis, so it is typically treated with hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement rather than fixation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young man is brought in after a motorbike crash. The AP pelvis shows widening of the pubic symphysis to 4 cm and he is hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
Apply a pelvic binder and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
Perform an isolated CT head before any intervention
Spring the pelvis to confirm instability
Order an outpatient MRI to look for occult fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Apply a pelvic binder and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An open-book injury with symphyseal diastasis can cause massive retroperitoneal haemorrhage and is life-threatening. A pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters plus resuscitation via the major haemorrhage protocol and urgent trauma/orthopaedic input is required. Springing the pelvis is contraindicated as it can worsen bleeding.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 70-year-old cannot weight-bear on the right hip after a fall. The AP pelvis is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same AP pelvis X-ray in one week
MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
Bone scan only if pain persists for six weeks
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A normal radiograph does not exclude a hip fracture. In a patient who cannot weight-bear, an occult fracture must be excluded with MRI (the most sensitive test), as delayed diagnosis increases morbidity and mortality.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old man attends the ED after a rugby tackle with his arm forced into abduction and external rotation. He supports the affected arm and cannot bring it across his chest. An AP shoulder radiograph shows the humeral head lying medial to and below the coracoid process. Which nerve is most at risk and must be documented before reduction?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Axillary nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a classic anterior (sub-coracoid) dislocation. The axillary nerve is most vulnerable — assess sensation over the "regimental badge" area of the lateral upper arm and deltoid function before and after reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old woman is brought in after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure with a painful shoulder held fixed in internal rotation; she cannot externally rotate it. The AP radiograph shows the humeral head appearing rounded and symmetrical ("light bulb" sign) with loss of the normal glenohumeral overlap. What is the most important next step?
options: Discharge with a sling as the AP is essentially normal
Obtain an axial or scapular-Y view to confirm the diagnosis
Request an urgent MRI of the shoulder
Immediately attempt closed reduction without further imaging
Arrange an outpatient ultrasound of the rotator cuff
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Obtain an axial or scapular-Y view to confirm the diagnosis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The history (seizure) plus the light-bulb sign strongly suggests a posterior dislocation — the classic missed diagnosis. A second orthogonal (axial/Y) view is essential to confirm the head is displaced posteriorly out of the glenoid.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand and has a painful, swollen shoulder. The radiograph shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus with two displaced parts. Which classification is used to grade this injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Neer classification
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Proximal humeral fractures are graded by the Neer classification, which counts the number of displaced parts (head, shaft, greater and lesser tuberosities). Garden is for femoral neck, Weber for ankle, Salter-Harris for physeal, and Gustilo-Anderson for open fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old man falls onto his shoulder playing rugby. The X-ray shows a mid-shaft clavicle fracture with the medial fragment elevated. Which muscle is responsible for the upward pull on the medial fragment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Sternocleidomastoid
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In middle-third fractures the medial fragment is elevated by the pull of sternocleidomastoid, while the lateral fragment is depressed by the weight of the arm — the classic displacement pattern.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old woman has an isolated, minimally displaced middle-third clavicle fracture with intact skin, normal distal pulses and normal neurology. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Urgent CT angiogram of the subclavian vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Broad arm sling and analgesia
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The great majority of uncomplicated middle-third fractures are managed conservatively with a broad arm sling and analgesia, mobilising as pain allows; most unite well. Surgery is reserved for complicated patterns.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old man is thrown from a motorbike and sustains a medial-third clavicle fracture. He reports difficulty breathing and there is fullness at the sternoclavicular region. Which complication must be excluded urgently?
options: Posterior displacement compressing the trachea and great vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posterior displacement compressing the trachea and great vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Medial-third fractures are rare and imply high-energy trauma. Posterior displacement can compress the trachea and mediastinal great vessels — a surgical emergency requiring urgent assessment (often CT) and senior/orthopaedic input.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls onto her shoulder and a radiograph shows a surgical neck fracture of the humerus. On examination she has weakness of shoulder abduction and reduced sensation over the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Axillary nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is at risk in surgical neck fractures. Injury causes deltoid weakness (abduction) and 'regimental badge' sensory loss over the lateral shoulder. The radial nerve relates to the mid-shaft, and the median nerve to supracondylar fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old man sustains a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft. He is subsequently found to have wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Which fracture eponym and nerve does this describe?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Holstein-Lewis fracture — radial nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft that classically entraps the radial nerve as it pierces the intermuscular septum, causing wrist drop and dorsal first web space sensory loss. The radial nerve runs in the spiral/radial groove of the humerus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 6-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and has a supracondylar humeral fracture. The hand is cool, pale, and the radial pulse is absent. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Discharge with a broad-arm sling and fracture clinic follow-up
Apply a full circumferential plaster cast and repeat X-ray in 1 week
Urgent reduction and orthopaedic input as a surgical emergency
Reassure and observe as pulses commonly return spontaneously over days
Prescribe analgesia and arrange outpatient MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent reduction and orthopaedic input as a surgical emergency
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A supracondylar fracture with an absent radial pulse and signs of ischaemia threatens the brachial artery and is a surgical emergency. It requires urgent reduction and orthopaedic involvement to restore perfusion and prevent compartment syndrome and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture. Delay or a circumferential cast risks limb-threatening ischaemia.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 45-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand and cannot fully extend his elbow. The lateral radiograph shows an elevated anterior fat pad and a visible posterior fat pad, but no fracture line. Which fracture is most likely?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Radial head fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In an adult, a fat pad sign (effusion) with no visible fracture most commonly represents an occult radial head fracture — the commonest occult adult elbow fracture after a FOOSH. It is managed as a fracture: sling and re-image/follow up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a paediatric lateral elbow film, the anterior humeral line passes through the anterior third of the capitellum rather than the middle third. What does this suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posteriorly displaced supracondylar fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The anterior humeral line should pass through the middle third of the capitellum. When it falls anteriorly, the capitellum has displaced posteriorly relative to the humerus — the hallmark of a posteriorly displaced supracondylar fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 6-year-old's elbow film appears to show a trochlear ossification centre but no medial (internal) epicondyle centre. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal — the trochlea can ossify first
Avulsed medial epicondyle displaced into the joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Avulsed medial epicondyle displaced into the joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: By the CRITOE sequence the medial epicondyle must ossify before the trochlea. A 'trochlea' without a preceding medial epicondyle means the medial epicondyle has avulsed and lies within the joint — that fragment is the displaced epicondyle, not the trochlea.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A child with a displaced supracondylar fracture has an absent radial pulse and cannot make the 'OK' sign. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Discharge with a sling and safety-net advice
Reassure and re-image in one week
Apply a full plaster cast and send home
Urgent orthopaedic referral for assessment of vascular and nerve injury
Prescribe analgesia and arrange outpatient physiotherapy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent orthopaedic referral for assessment of vascular and nerve injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A supracondylar fracture can injure the brachial artery and median nerve (classically the anterior interosseous branch — loss of the 'OK' sign). An absent pulse signals vascular compromise, a surgical emergency requiring urgent orthopaedic input, not discharge or delayed follow-up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old falls and an X-ray shows a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna. On the lateral elbow view, a line drawn along the radial neck does not pass through the centre of the capitellum. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Monteggia fracture-dislocation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A proximal ulnar fracture combined with a disrupted radiocapitellar line (radial head dislocation) defines a Monteggia injury. MUGR: Monteggia = Ulna. In adults this typically requires ORIF.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A distal radial shaft fracture is seen on X-ray. Which additional finding would confirm a Galeazzi fracture-dislocation?
options: Dislocation of the radial head at the elbow
Widening/dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
A fracture of the proximal ulna
Buckling of the distal radial cortex only
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Widening/dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Galeazzi = distal Radius fracture with DRUJ disruption (MUGR: Galeazzi = Radius). Radial head dislocation and proximal ulnar fracture belong to Monteggia; cortical buckling alone suggests a paediatric buckle fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Six hours after casting a both-bone forearm fracture, a patient reports severe pain that is worse than expected and markedly increased on passive finger extension. Distal pulses are present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and prescribe stronger oral analgesia
Repeat the X-ray to check alignment
Elevate the limb and review in the morning
Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and consideration of fasciotomy
Remove the cast and discharge with advice
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and consideration of fasciotomy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome; pulses are often preserved until late. This is a limb-threatening surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy, not reassurance or delay.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 72-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and a “dinner fork” clinical deformity. Which fracture is this?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Colles' fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Colles' is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement/angulation producing the dinner-fork deformity, classically after a FOOSH in an osteoporotic elderly woman. Smith's is volar (garden spade); Barton's is intra-articular.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a lateral wrist radiograph, the lunate is seated normally on the distal radius but the capitate is dislocated dorsally and no longer articulates with the lunate. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Perilunate dislocation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In a perilunate dislocation the radius–lunate alignment is preserved but the capitate dislocates (usually dorsally) off the lunate. In a lunate dislocation it is the lunate itself that tips volar off the radius (“spilled teacup”). Both are orthopaedic emergencies.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which set of values represents the approximately normal distal radius parameters used to assess adequacy of reduction?
options: Radial height ~22 mm, inclination ~11°, volar tilt ~5°
Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~22°, volar tilt ~11°
Radial height ~5 mm, inclination ~30°, dorsal tilt ~22°
Radial height ~30 mm, inclination ~11°, volar tilt ~22°
Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~11°, dorsal tilt ~11°
Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~11°, dorsal tilt ~11°
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~22°, volar tilt ~11°
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The standard teaching values are radial height ~11 mm, radial inclination ~22° and volar (palmar) tilt ~11°. In Colles' the volar tilt is reversed to dorsal tilt — restoring these parameters is the goal of reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand playing football. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial compression of the thumb. A dedicated scaphoid series is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with advice that it is a simple sprain
Immobilise in a thumb spica (scaphoid/futuro splint) and arrange repeat imaging in 10–14 days or MRI
Prescribe analgesia and arrange routine physiotherapy
Request a bone scan in 6 weeks
Apply a full above-elbow cast and review in 3 months
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immobilise in a thumb spica (scaphoid/futuro splint) and arrange repeat imaging in 10–14 days or MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal initial film represents a frequently occult scaphoid fracture. Treat as a fracture: immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray at 10–14 days or MRI, which is most sensitive). Discharging as a sprain risks AVN and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which anatomical feature explains why a proximal pole scaphoid fracture is at high risk of avascular necrosis?
options: The scaphoid has a rich dual arterial supply from the ulnar and radial arteries
The scaphoid is entirely covered in periosteum with abundant vessels
The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering the distal pole from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
The scaphoid receives its blood supply directly from the interosseous membrane
Blood enters at the proximal pole from the anterior interosseous artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering the distal pole from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters at the distal pole and perfuses the bone distal-to-proximal (retrograde). A proximal pole or waist fracture therefore devascularises the proximal fragment, causing AVN and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about the initial X-ray in suspected scaphoid fracture is correct?
options: A normal scaphoid series reliably excludes a fracture
The fracture is frequently occult (not visible) on the initial film despite a correct scaphoid series
A single PA wrist view is the definitive investigation
CT is contraindicated because of radiation to the wrist
A visible fracture line is required before any immobilisation is applied
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The fracture is frequently occult (not visible) on the initial film despite a correct scaphoid series
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible initially; a normal film does not exclude the diagnosis. This is why clinical suspicion (snuffbox tenderness) mandates immobilisation and further imaging (repeat X-ray, MRI, or CT) rather than discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old man attends ED after punching a wall. X-ray shows a fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck with volar angulation. On examination his little finger overlaps the ring finger when he makes a fist. What is the most important management priority?
options: Discharge with buddy strapping as angulation is well tolerated
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation of all metacarpal neck fractures
Reassure and review in fracture clinic in 6 weeks with no intervention
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Correction of the rotational deformity
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Volar angulation at the 5th metacarpal neck is often tolerated because of the mobile CMC joint, but rotational malalignment (finger scissoring/overlap on flexion) causes functional impairment and must be corrected. Rotation is a clinical diagnosis, checked by ensuring the fingers point toward the scaphoid on flexion.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old presents with pain at the base of the thumb after a fall. X-ray shows an intra-articular fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal with a small volar-ulnar fragment remaining in place while the shaft is displaced proximally. Which muscle is responsible for the displacement?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Abductor pollicis longus
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a Bennett's fracture-dislocation. The small volar-ulnar fragment is anchored by the anterior oblique ligament, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally and radially, making the injury unstable.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 25-year-old attends ED with a 1 cm laceration over the knuckle of the right hand sustained during a fight. He reports his fist struck the other man's face. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Primary closure with sutures and discharge
Steri-strips and a tetanus booster only
Thorough exploration/washout and antibiotics, left open, with hand referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Thorough exploration/washout and antibiotics, left open, with hand referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A knuckle wound from a punch is a 'fight bite' (clenched-fist injury) and must be treated as a human-bite wound. It risks septic arthritis and extensor tenosynovitis. It requires washout, antibiotics (e.g. co-amoxiclav), and must never be closed primarily; hand-surgery involvement is standard.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient cannot actively extend the tip of their finger after a ball struck the fingertip. X-ray shows a small avulsion fragment at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Mallet finger
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Mallet finger is a bony avulsion of the extensor tendon at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx, producing a drooped DIP that cannot be actively extended. A dorsal avulsion flake is seen on the lateral view.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skier falls onto an outstretched hand with a ski pole, forcing the thumb into abduction. There is pain and instability at the thumb MCP joint, and X-ray shows a small avulsion at the base of the proximal phalanx. Which structure is injured?
options: Radial collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
Volar plate of the thumb IP joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is gamekeeper's/skier's thumb: injury to the ulnar collateral ligament at the thumb MCP joint (± bony avulsion) from forced abduction. It causes MCP instability and, if a displaced Stener lesion is present, requires surgical repair.
